what: A route for someone leaving computing
note: Six routes in, and none out. People do leave this field, for good reasons, and the decision deserves the same treatment as entering. This edition has no evidence base on where they go or how it works out, so it offers no route rather than an encouraging guess.

what: The computing figure from ten of the eleven confirmed graduate-earnings publishers
note: Appendix G confirms eleven publishers of course-level graduate earnings matched to tax or register records, and every one of them breaks its figures out by field. Only Ireland's computing number is printed in this book. The other ten are named, with what they cover and how to reach them, and the reader is sent to open their own. That is work this edition did not do rather than data that does not exist.

what: Whether the countries with no graduate-earnings dataset truly have none
note: No such dataset was found for seventeen of the markets this book serves. Those searches ran in English against national portals, and a dataset published only in a national language would have been missed. The claim is that none was found, which describes this edition rather than those countries.

what: Regulator findings on training providers in six of seventeen markets
note: Appendix G names a regulator with jurisdiction in seventeen countries. In eleven of them something has happened to a provider, though only eight of those were fines from a consumer regulator. In one the regulator looked and found no breach. In the remaining five no published action was found at all. Several of those bodies publish almost nothing in English and resolve complaints by mediation, so the absence is very likely about publication rather than about behaviour.

what: How many schools currently submit outcomes to an independent audit
note: No primary source gave a current membership count for the one widely used audit standard. The chapter asks the reader to put the question to the school instead, which works whatever the number is.

what: How much of software testing employment is manual, and how much is automation
note: The Bureau projects software quality assurance analysts and testers as one occupation, growing 10.0% to 2034. That code counts people who test by hand and people who write test automation together, and publishes no split between them. This book argues that purely manual testing is closing as a career while automation work is not, and the occupation figure can neither confirm nor contradict that, because it is their average. No published source separates the two.

what: The size and pay of these jobs outside the United States
note: The counts and the pay ranges in this chapter are American. The United States runs the best occupational survey in the world, and most countries publish nothing at this level of detail. Appendix G records which ones come close. A reader in India, Nigeria or Brazil should read the shape of these findings and not the amounts.

what: What share of job postings become jobs
note: The direction findings in this chapter are built on job postings, because postings are the only thing published fast enough to describe a market this year. No job board publishes what share of its listings result in a hire. A posting can be duplicated, left up after the role is filled, or never filled at all. So the direction of those numbers is evidence and the level is not.

what: Graduate outcomes behind the entry-level contraction
note: The finding that entry-level hiring is shrinking rests on posting seniority, not on what happened to graduates. Those are different measurements. The graduate unemployment figures in this chapter come from a different instrument again, and cover one country.

what: School system subject rules outside eleven countries
note: This chapter now works through India, the United Kingdom, the United States, Germany, the International Baccalaureate, Egypt, Bangladesh, Pakistan, the Philippines, Indonesia and Vietnam. Nigeria and Brazil remain uncovered and both send large numbers of students into computing. The method in the first half of the chapter is written to work anywhere. The worked examples are not.

what: Whether the rule that mathematics is the binding subject holds outside these eleven
note: It holds in all eleven systems described here, which is the strongest pattern in this chapter. Eleven is not a sample of the world's school systems, and the countries were chosen by where readers are rather than at random. So the rule is a well-supported generalisation and not a measured one.

what: What happens to people who start a route and stop
note: Every figure in this chapter describes people who finished something. No published source follows the person who left a degree in year two, or stopped a certificate ladder after the first exam. That group is large and it is invisible, and it is exactly the group a reader is trying not to join.

what: Apprenticeship availability outside the United Kingdom and Germany
note: The two apprenticeship systems described here are the two this edition could describe. Many countries run something similar under another name, and some run nothing at all. A reader elsewhere cannot tell from this chapter which case they are in.

This chapter recommends a route that depends on employers paying for study later. That happens. How often it happens, in which countries, and how many people actually use it are all unknown here. The recommendation rests on the route existing, not on a measured rate of take-up.

what: Credit transfer and early-credit routes outside the United States
note: The chapter shows how to make the same degree cheaper by starting at a lower-cost institution and transferring. The mechanism is described from the United States community college system. Which countries run an equivalent, what it is called there, and what it saves are not compiled. The chapter gives an instruction that works anywhere instead of a figure that works in one place.

what: Whether complaining achieves anything in the six markets with no published case
note: Appendix G now names a consumer regulator, its statute and its filing route for seventeen countries, which closes the gap this chapter carried in the first edition. In eleven, a specific action against a provider can be named. In five none was found and in one the regulator found no breach, so the book can say where to complain and cannot say what complaining is worth there.

what: What to check before signing an employment contract, outside India
note: Service bonds now have a section here and a worked treatment in Appendix H, for one country. Probation, notice, non-competition clauses and what total pay actually contains all differ by country, and sixteen other origin markets have none of it compiled. Contract norms by country sit outside this edition's scope.

what: How long each stage of the sequence actually takes
note: The timings in this chapter are read off the 46 profiles in Book B and the gates described in Chapter 25. They are not measured. Nobody publishes time-to-first-job for almost any computing field, which is why 35 of the 46 profiles declare an entry-time gap. The stage lengths here are therefore the book's own reading of its own data, and they are stated as rough on purpose. Treat them as an order of magnitude.

what: Any test of whether this book's framework actually picks well
note: The ten dimensions have never been scored against an outcome. No cohort was followed, no retrodiction was run, and no prediction was scored. The obvious test is to apply the framework as of 2015 and check its picks against 2026, and this edition did not run it, because whoever ran it would already know how 2026 turned out and would be marking their own homework with the answers in front of them. Nor can the claim be tested against published data: it would need somebody to follow two groups of entrants for five years, and no such study exists or is being funded. The chapter says so, and registers five dated checks on the market machinery instead — two that could go wrong and three that probably will not, labelled as such, with a rule forbidding the easy three from averaging out a failure in the other two. Until somebody runs the cohort study, the framework is a well-organised argument rather than a tested instrument, and the book should be read as one.

what: How many jobs exist, for the roles a US occupation survey does count
note: Chapter 13 prints employment counts for seventeen computing occupations from the American survey, and 39 of 46 profiles still read "not established" for market size. The counts are not wired into the profiles because no profile carries an occupation code, and this book copies those codes from research rather than inferring them: a guessed code is checkable, authoritative-looking and wrong, which is the failure Part I teaches readers to detect. This edition planned to close it by matching each profile's name against the American job-title file, which lists the titles employers actually use against each code, and called that a download rather than a judgement. The download was done. It is a judgement. The file lists "Maintainer" under machinery maintenance and "Quantitative Trader" under securities sales, so a copied code can be exact, official and still describe a different job. One profile in thirty-nine came through it cleanly. Copying a code stops you inventing an occupation; it does not tell you the occupation is yours.

what: The complete role lists from the taxonomies this book cites
note: Four public frameworks are used here to prove that roles exist. This edition read their structures and the specific codes it prints, not their full contents. So the enumeration in Appendix D is a floor rather than a ceiling, and the chapter says which parts were read.

what: How many of these jobs exist, for most of the 46
note: Every profile now carries a "how many jobs" line, and 39 of 46 read "not established". Seven have a count because somebody publishes one: quantum, computational chemistry, bioinformatics, geospatial, tenure-track academia, junior UX and Epic. For the rest no source counts openings or headcount at the level of a named computing role, in any country. This book teaches readers to ask "percent of what?" and could not answer it about most of its own recommendations until an outside review said so.

Every framework used here publishes in English. National classifications exist in many other languages and were not consulted. A role that is named and counted only in, say, Japanese or Portuguese statistics is invisible to this book.

what: Everything a profile would contain, for every role in this chapter
note: This is the only chapter in Book B with no profiles, and the absence is the finding. A profile needs pay data at grade 3 and entry data at grade 2. A role that appeared eighteen months ago has neither, because nobody has yet done it long enough to be surveyed. Writing profiles anyway would mean inventing the numbers, in the part of the book most likely to be acted on by someone in a hurry.

what: Whether any of these roles will still exist in five years
note: The chapter records what emerged and what was absorbed by August 2026. It has no way to tell which of the emerging categories becomes a durable occupation and which is absorbed in turn. The one honest thing it can do is give the reader the test, which is the last section.

what: Emergence outside the United States and Europe
note: Almost every measurement here is from United States postings. New role categories usually appear in one market first and spread, but this edition cannot say which of these have spread, how far, or how fast.

Every ladder in this chapter is compiled from what each profile says about how people enter that role. That evidences the direction of the move. It does not evidence the rate. No source found publishes what share of help desk workers reach a security role, or how long the median move takes, or how many never move at all. The chapter says which way the ladders run. It cannot tell you the odds of climbing one.

what: Ladders between roles this book does not profile
note: These ladders connect the 46 roles in Book B. Appendix D indexes every job title the book can place, which is a much smaller set than the roles that exist. A ladder running through a role the index does not hold is invisible to this chapter, and the method at the end of the chapter is the only tool it can offer for finding it.

what: How often the sideways move fails
note: The profiles describe how people who arrived in a role arrived. Nobody publishes what happened to the people who took the same first rung and stayed on it. That group is larger than the group described here, and this book cannot size it.

what: Independent measurement of what any certificate adds to pay
note: Every pay premium in this chapter comes from a party with an interest in the answer: a training body, a sector job site, or people who hold the certificate reporting their own pay. No source found compares certificate holders against matched non-holders doing the same job. So this chapter can rank certificates by who controls access, which is structural and checkable, and cannot rank them by what they pay.

what: Saturation figures for certificates other than Salesforce
note: The Salesforce case is the one place this book has a measured supply-and-demand ratio. The same mechanism almost certainly operates on other buyable certificates, and this edition has not measured it anywhere else. The reader is given the mechanism and told to check their own market, because that is what the evidence supports.

what: Renewal costs for enterprise vendors that do not publish a price
note: The ten-year table covers eighteen certificates whose issuers publish their prices. Several large vendors do not, among them ServiceNow, Palo Alto Networks, Splunk, Fortinet, CREST and the gated platforms in category one. Their figures circulate only on aggregator sites, which Chapter 5 grades 4, so they are left out rather than printed at a lower grade. A vendor that will not publish its price is itself telling you something.

what: Any timing at all for the argument in this afterword
note: The afterword reasons from the structure of why jobs exist, and from what has happened to other kinds of work before. Neither of those is a measurement. It cannot say when a field thins out, or whether this one will, and it says so in its own text rather than in a footnote. By the book's own grading it is the weakest evidence in the book.

what: Whether cheaper computing thins this field out or enlarges it
note: The afterword's mechanism is observed at the level of a single role, in Chapter 29, and the step from there to the whole field is an extrapolation of exactly the kind Chapter 4 warns about. The same chapter records four kinds of work that appeared over the same two years. The obvious reply to the afterword is that each previous round of computing getting cheaper was followed by more computing work rather than less, and this book has no measurement that settles it either way. So the afterword argues its side and prints the reply beside it rather than deciding between them.

what: Pay for any named computing role in India
note: The national labour survey publishes earnings by occupation group, not by specialisation. Institutional placement medians are reported by the institution being judged. Aggregator sites are grade 4 and excluded everywhere else in this book, so they are excluded here. No source at grade 3 or better gives pay for a named Indian computing role, which leaves the book's largest market with the weakest pay evidence in it.

what: The methodology behind the apprenticeship employment figures
note: The first edition of this annex said no evaluation existed. It does, and the government reports 72% and 74% employment on completion. This book has read the government's summary rather than the underlying evaluations, and one official wording says apprentices "reported receiving offers", which is weaker than a verified placement. The sample, the definition of employment and the timing all need checking before those figures are treated as settled.

what: What each employer type pays, relative to the others
note: This is now a confirmed absence with a known cause rather than a failed search. Indian law compels a listed company to publish the pay of its median employee, so the services side is measurable. A capability centre is an unlisted private subsidiary and owes no such figure, and its foreign parent can only report a global median. One side of the comparison is required by law and the other cannot exist. Consultancy surveys put the premium at 12% to 20% without publishing a method.

what: An India-only pay figure from any of these companies
note: Every median in this annex is global. These firms employ heavily outside India and onsite staff earn far more, so each figure is pulled upward by people who do not live here. None of the eight reports read for this edition splits its median by country. That is the single most valuable thing still missing, because it is the difference between a number about an employer and a number about India.

what: Why the senior grades look the way they do
note: One large employer publishes near parity at junior level and about four men to one woman at senior level, with equal median pay at the bottom. A single year's snapshot cannot separate people leaving from who was hired a decade ago, and both would produce that picture. Nothing found distinguishes them, and guessing would be the exact reasoning error Chapter 5 tells readers to refuse.

The cohort here is eight listed services firms. Their medians span a wide range, and the mid-sized specialists sit well above the largest firms. That is a real finding and it is not the comparison readers want, which remains impossible for the reason given below.

what: Product companies and startups, separately from fintech
note: Neither headcount nor attrition is published for Indian product-software firms on their own. They are folded in with fintech and e-commerce, which churn at 25% to 28% and pull any combined figure upward. The archetype most often held up as aspirational is the one with no numbers.

Two country annexes exist, this one and Appendix I for Nigeria. Brazil, the Philippines, Indonesia, Pakistan, Vietnam, Bangladesh, Egypt, Mexico, Kenya, Poland, Ukraine, Turkey, Argentina, Colombia and South Africa need the same treatment and do not have it. Fifteen, not sixteen: this list named Nigeria until August 2026, after Appendix I had already been written.

what: Any occupation-level pay figure for computing work in Nigeria
note: The national labour force survey is a serious instrument and publishes participation, unemployment, informality and the split between wage and self-employment. It does not publish earnings by occupation, so there is no official figure for what any computing role pays. This was searched for directly and confirmed absent rather than assumed.

what: How many Nigerians earn abroad on remote contracts
note: This is the single most important economic fact about Nigerian computing careers and nobody has sized it. Remittance flows through licensed operators are published, but they cover everybody sending money home, not developers billing foreign clients.

what: Headcount at the fintech companies that dominate the sector
note: One telecoms operator discloses its staff numbers, and that is the only clean employer figure in this annex. The fintech firms most graduates want to join publish nothing comparable.

what: Emigration volume, and where people go
note: Nigeria has no exit-visa system and publishes little emigration data. The route to a real number is visa issuance published by destination countries, and this edition has not compiled it.

what: Pay for any named computing role in five of these six countries
note: Only the Philippines publishes a government wage figure that names a computing occupation. Vietnam publishes wages at the broadest occupation group, where every professional is counted together. Indonesia collapses everything into eight groups and computing disappears inside professionals and technicians. Pakistan, Bangladesh and Egypt publish sector or economy-wide averages only. So for five of the six there is no role-level pay figure at any grade this book accepts, and the aggregate figures printed here must not be read as salaries.

what: Whether the export receipts can be turned into a per-person figure
note: They cannot, and the temptation is strong enough to state it. Central bank export receipts are the best recorded earnings data these countries have. They are aggregate flows of foreign currency. Dividing one by a headcount would produce a number that looks like average pay and is not, because nobody publishes how many people the receipts belong to.

No regulator in any of the six publishes a named decision against a training provider for false job-placement claims. That was searched for in the national language in every case and confirmed absent rather than assumed. It is a negative finding about the published record, not proof that no enforcement has ever happened.

what: A reconciled Egyptian sector wage figure
note: The statistics office's information and communication sector wage is quoted at EGP 12,897 a month for 2024 and EGP 19,179 for 2023 in secondary reporting. A sector average that falls by a third in a year needs checking against the original bulletin before either figure is relied on. This edition prints both and trusts neither.
